policy_title: Tackle Asylum Backlog and Allow Asylum Seekers to Work
stated: Tackle the asylum backlog by establishing a dedicated unit to improve the speed and quality of asylum decision-making, introducing a service standard of three months for all but the most complex asylum claims to be processed, and speeding up returns of those without a right to stay. Lift the ban on asylum seekers working if they have been waiting for a decision for more than three months.

source.quote: Tackle the asylum backlog by establishing a dedicated unit to improve the speed and quality of asylum decision-making, introducing a service standard of three months for all but the most complex asylum claims to be processed, and speeding up returns of those without a right to stay. Lift the ban on asylum seekers working if they have been waiting for a decision for more than three months, enabling them to support themselves, integrate in their communities and contribute to the economy.

bearing_set.reason: Lifting the work ban for asylum seekers waiting more than three months directly affects whether a defined group can earn income and support themselves — a real verdict on work access and pay.

The current bar on working is a legal restriction on a specific group's autonomy; removing it bears on their equal treatment and legal rights under the immigration framework, squarely within O9's scope.

The returns component ('speeding up returns of those without a right to stay') directly bears on national security and border-integrity posture, with a concrete mechanism: faster removal of those who have no lawful basis to remain reduces irregular presence and associated security risks.

Lifting the existing work ban removes a state-imposed restriction on asylum seekers' ability to earn a living; this is a direct reduction in state coercion over a defined population, improving personal liberty regardless of wider policy intent.

The policy has two countervailing fiscal mechanisms with non-negligible scale: a new dedicated processing unit carries setup and running costs, while allowing asylum seekers to work reduces reliance on Section 95 asylum support (currently costing billions annually) — the net direction is contested but material enough to earn a real verdict.

membership_note: Four fundamentals across two distinct sub-policies (processing reform and work-ban lift). O13 excluded — aggregate labour-supply effect is real but marginal relative to the UK workforce. O15 excluded — integration-via-work mechanism is plausible but insufficiently direct to clear the non-negligible bar. O5 excluded — faster returns have a border-order dimension, but the policy is primarily an efficiency/due-process measure, not a security or enforcement measure.
